title: Words for a massacre
hookLine: a tiger among the sheep: in Asa, Guru Nanak's hymn on the invasion asks the Master of the flock to answer for the ordinary people who suffered

cards: Two heavyweights step into a ring. Both trained, both chose to be there, and when one goes down, the crowd groans but nobody calls it a crime. Now change the scene.
A tiger comes down a hillside into a field of sheep. Nobody chose this fight. The sheep can't hit back.
Guru Nanak sang exactly that difference, about an invasion of Punjab, in a hymn in Raga Asa. Sikhs call his hymns on that invasion the Babarvani.

teach.b: First, the name. Babarvani puts the name of Babur, the invader, beside vani, words: a small group of Guru Nanak's hymns about what Babur's armies did.
One of them even uses the phrase for the invader's sway: Babar vaanee spread. Second, the hymn itself, in paraphrase. Khurasan is taken under the invader's hand, and Hindustan is put in terror.
Then the Rahao turns to God: Creator, you are the Master of all. If the powerful strike the powerful, the mind holds no grievance.
And the next verse holds the ring and the field together: but if a powerful tiger falls on a flock, the Master of the flock must answer for it. Guru Nanak doesn't grieve for kings losing to kings.
He grieves for the flock: farmers, families, people who never chose a side and couldn't fight back. Third, notice where he takes that grief. Not to the invader, not to a crowd.
To God, as the Master who is answerable.
Earlier on this path we heard this hymn's cry, did you feel no pain? Today, hear the logic under it.
If God is Master of all, the flock is God's flock, and its suffering is not a footnote. It is the point. Fourth, the hymn says the jewel of the land was spoiled, and no one cared for the dead.
These are words for a massacre, kept in scripture and still sung, so the ones without power are remembered in the Guru's own voice.

how: The Babarvani hymns are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib like any other Gurbani; some Sikhs turn to them when remembering victims of violence and speaking about justice for ordinary people.

games.q: the hymn sets two kinds of violence side by side. which one does it say the Master of the flock must answer for?
o: a powerful tiger falling on a flock.
games.why: if the powerful strike the powerful, the mind holds no grievance. but if a tiger falls on a flock, the Master must answer for it.

practice: Bring to mind people living through war today, not the leaders or the armies but the flock: a family packing in a hurry, a child at a shelter.
If you pray, pray for them in your own tradition's way or say Waheguru on each breath out; if you don't, keep them in mind with each breath, as if sitting beside them.
And if this touches a loss of your own and feels too heavy, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach your local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Babarvani. Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion, which grieve for the flock, not the kings, and bring that grief to the Master of all. Today's word.

orig.note: khasmai: to the Master, the owner of the flock; the hymn says the Master must answer for it.

carryVoice: Your line: he named the pain. The flock is not a footnote. Be gentle with yourself today.
